paragraphs: Classification systems often assume that all possible categories are known in advance and appear at roughly comparable rates. The paper addresses a different setting: some categories are common, many are rare, and new categories may appear as observations arrive. Nonparametric Bayesian models accommodate this open set of possibilities, but their implementation and computational demands can make them difficult to use.

The authors transfer the assumptions of such a Bayesian model into a neural network through metalearning. They simulate data using a nonparametric Bayesian prior, then train a sequence model to perform the associated inference. Across this training experience, the network learns how to process successive observations without requiring a fixed, closed list of classes.

Experiments show comparable or better inference performance than particle filter methods, alongside faster execution and simpler use. The contribution is a way to retain useful modeling assumptions while changing the machinery that carries out inference. The resulting neural circuit learns to handle an open class set through training rather than explicitly executing the original Bayesian procedure.
neurips-2024-a-metalearned-neural-circui.tldr: A sequence model trained on simulated Bayesian data learns efficient inference over an open set of classes.

paragraphs: The paper uses logic puzzles to investigate whether causal language modeling can learn search and reasoning. Sudoku requires more than choosing a plausible next number: a solver must select an empty cell, identify an applicable strategy, and sometimes combine several deductions before committing to a value. This makes the sequence of intermediate decisions central to the task.

The authors train Transformers on logical steps produced by a solver. Their model solves 94.21% of Sudoku puzzles completely correctly and, in an extension to Zebra puzzles, achieves 92.04%. In the reported training setting, logical step sequences are necessary: without them, the Transformers fail to learn Sudoku. That result ties success to the structure of supervision used in these experiments.

The authors also examine the trained models' internal representations using linear probes. These probes recover information about which values remain possible in a cell. Together with puzzle-solving performance, this suggests that the models develop internal representations useful for reasoning, rather than merely producing correct final answers without any detectable representation of intermediate possibilities.
neurips-2024-causal-language-modeling-ca.tldr: Transformers trained on logical solving steps learn Sudoku and Zebra puzzles and internally represent candidate cell values.

paragraphs: Materials knowledge is scattered across scientific papers, making it difficult to bring together information relevant to discovery. The paper addresses this organization problem by constructing a Materials Knowledge Graph from a decade of high-quality research. Its aim is to turn dispersed textual information into a structured resource that supports integration and further analysis.

The construction process combines natural language processing with large language models to extract structured triples: linked pieces of information that describe relationships. A designed ontology specifies how the extracted knowledge is organized, including labels such as Name, Formula, and Application. The resulting graph contains 162,605 nodes and 731,772 edges, giving the extracted literature a shared relational structure.

The authors apply network-based algorithms to support link prediction and report reduced reliance on traditional experimental methods. The practical significance lies in making relationships across the literature available for computational exploration. Organizing names, formulas, applications, and their connections in a common framework also provides a foundation for more sophisticated materials knowledge graphs.
neurips-2024-construction-and-applicatio.tldr: A language-model-assisted knowledge graph organizes materials literature into structured relationships for integration and link prediction.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly connects two kinds of data, such as pictures and captions. When several modalities are available, applying a two-modality method separately to each pair can miss information carried by their joint relationship. The paper identifies this problem for pairwise CLIP and introduces Symile to learn relationships involving any number of modalities together.

Symile supplies a training objective that can work with different model architectures while producing a separate representation for each modality. Its mathematical foundation is a lower bound on total correlation, a measure of shared statistical dependence across multiple variables. The authors also show that representations of any subset of modalities form a sufficient statistic for predicting the remaining modalities.

Experiments find that Symile outperforms pairwise CLIP on classification and retrieval across modalities, including when some modalities are missing. Evaluations include 33 million multilingual image, text, and audio samples and clinical data combining chest X-rays, electrocardiograms, and laboratory measurements. These findings support learning joint relationships directly when useful information extends beyond individual pairs.
neurips-2024-contrasting-with-symile-sim.tldr: Symile learns joint relationships across multiple modalities and outperforms pairwise CLIP in the reported classification and retrieval experiments.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers need structural guidance to decide which nodes should attend to one another. Existing approaches can struggle with relationships that span long distances or reflect communities and hierarchies. This paper introduces Hierarchical Distance Structural Encoding, or HDSE, to represent distances through multiple levels of a graph's organization.

The method integrates these distance descriptions into attention, giving the model information about hierarchical relationships when it computes attention scores. HDSE can also be used alongside other positional encodings, allowing it to supplement existing descriptions of graph structure. For large graphs, the authors introduce a high-level variant that guides linear Transformers toward the graph's hierarchy.

The paper provides theoretical results supporting improvements in expressivity and generalization. Its empirical evaluation covers graph classification and regression on seven graph-level datasets, together with node classification on eleven large graphs. The reported performance supports the value of representing organization at multiple scales: local connectivity alone may leave out structure that helps a Transformer learn useful graph representations.
neurips-2024-enhancing-graph-transformer.tldr: HDSE gives graph Transformers hierarchical distance information, with theoretical support and strong results across graph and node prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems involve reconstructing an image from incomplete or altered measurements. A flow-based generative model can supply a prior describing which images are plausible, making it attractive for maximum-a-posteriori estimation. The obstacle is computational: evaluating the required image log-likelihood involves backpropagating through an ordinary differential equation solver, which can be prohibitively slow for high-dimensional images.

The paper proposes an iterative method that approximates this estimation problem more efficiently. Its mathematical starting point is that the overall objective can be approximated by a sum of local estimation objectives, with their number matching the number of function evaluations. Using Tweedie's formula, the authors derive gradient steps that optimize these local objectives sequentially.

The method is evaluated on super-resolution, deblurring, inpainting, and compressed sensing. The authors demonstrate that it can outperform other methods based on flow matching. The contribution is therefore an efficient approximation strategy for using learned flow priors in reconstruction, supported by both a mathematical justification and experiments across several kinds of linear measurement problems.
neurips-2024-flow-priors-for-linear-inve.tldr: Sequential local approximations make flow-based image priors more practical for solving linear inverse problems.

paragraphs: Preference training often labels one response as the winner and another as the loser. This paper argues that such binary labels discard variation between people's preferences. It introduces soft preference labels that describe a distribution of preference, allowing a response pair to express anything from a strong preference to an almost even split.

The authors modify Direct Preference Optimization by using a weighted geometric average of output likelihoods in its loss. The weighting makes the training loss shrink toward zero as the responses become equally preferred. This reduces the pressure to force a clear winner from an ambiguous comparison and is designed to mitigate over-optimization and mismatch between the training objective and the preference information.

Experiments simulate soft labels using feedback from language models. Geometric averaging consistently improves performance on the alignment benchmarks studied and produces more preferable responses than binary labels. Gains are especially pronounced when most labels express only modest confidence. The evidence therefore supports preserving preference strength in training, with the reported tests specifically using AI-generated preference feedback.
neurips-2024-geometric-averaged-preferen.tldr: A geometric-average modification to DPO uses soft preferences to reduce training pressure on ambiguous comparisons and improve reported alignment results.

paragraphs: When several parts of a system interact, predicting each time series independently can miss information about how the whole system evolves. The challenge becomes harder when measurements arrive at irregular times. This paper develops a model that learns both the relationships among components and their behavior through continuous time.

The relationships are represented by a directed acyclic graph describing conditional dependencies between components. The graph is learned together with a continuous-time model that parameterizes solution curves of ordinary differential equations. This joint construction connects a description of which components depend on others with a description of how their values change, rather than treating those two modeling tasks separately.

The authors call the resulting method a graph neural flow and evaluate it on tasks including forecasting and time series classification. They report substantial improvements over methods without graphs and graph methods that do not model conditional dependencies. These findings support the predictive value of the chosen dependency structure; the abstract describes it as a form of causal notation rather than reporting experimental identification of causal effects.
neurips-2024-graph-neural-flows-for-unve.tldr: Graph neural flows jointly learn conditional dependencies and continuous-time dynamics to improve prediction from irregularly sampled time series.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn decision-making policies from a fixed dataset, without gathering new experience through interaction. Data augmentation can help, but smoothing the observed state-action region does not necessarily improve the quality of the available behavior. GTA addresses this distinction by aiming to generate trajectories that combine higher rewards with plausible system dynamics.

The method uses a diffusion model to transform existing trajectories. It first adds noise to part of their structure and then denoises them while conditioning on an amplified return value. Classifier-free guidance steers this reconstruction toward the higher-return target. Starting from recorded trajectories connects generation to existing data, while the return conditioning gives the augmentation an explicit direction for improvement.

The authors report that GTA improves widely used offline reinforcement learning algorithms across tasks with different challenges. They also analyze the augmented data and find improvements in its quality. Together, these results support trajectory augmentation as a way to improve the learning material itself, with GTA functioning as a general data augmentation strategy for offline policy learning.
neurips-2024-gta-generative-trajectory-a.tldr: GTA uses return-guided diffusion to augment offline trajectories toward higher rewards and plausible dynamics, improving reported policy-learning results.

paragraphs: L4GM reconstructs an animated 3D object from a video showing it from a single viewpoint. The fourth dimension is time: the output describes a changing object rather than one static shape. The authors report that reconstruction takes about a second in a single feed-forward pass, making speed a central part of the contribution.

The model builds on LGM, a pretrained reconstruction model that represents objects with 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. L4GM adds temporal self-attention to learn consistency across frames and trains using rendered views at each timestep. It initially predicts Gaussian representations at a low frame rate, then uses a learned interpolation model to produce intermediate representations and smoother motion.

Training relies on a large synthetic collection of animated objects: 44,000 objects and 110,000 animations rendered from 48 viewpoints, yielding 12 million videos. Despite training only on synthetic data, the authors demonstrate good generalization to videos captured in the wild. The result shows how multiview synthetic supervision and temporal modeling can support rapid animated reconstruction from single-view input.
neurips-2024-l4gm-large-4d-gaussian-reco.tldr: L4GM turns a single-view video into an animated 3D Gaussian representation in about a second, using synthetic multiview training.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks update each node using messages from neighboring nodes. Their memory requirements therefore grow with the number of graph edges, which becomes costly for large graphs that are not very sparse. This paper changes the representation on which learning operates to reduce that dependence on individual connections.

The authors approximate the original graph using an intersecting community graph, a combination of overlapping cliques. Their key observation is that the number of communities required for approximation does not depend on graph size. A new constructive form of the Weak Graph Regularity Lemma provides a way to build this approximation for any input graph.

The paper then introduces a learning algorithm that works directly on the community representation with time and memory linear in the number of nodes. This shifts the learning cost away from the potentially much larger edge count. Experiments on node classification and spatio-temporal data demonstrate applicability, supporting a different computational pipeline for learning on large, non-sparse graphs through an explicitly approximated representation.
neurips-2024-learning-on-large-graphs-us.tldr: Approximating graphs with overlapping communities enables a learning algorithm whose time and memory scale linearly with nodes rather than edges.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning all parameters of a large language model requires substantial GPU memory. Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, reduces that burden but restricts the parameter search to a low-rank subspace. This paper explores another route after observing a consistent imbalance in weight norms across layers during LoRA fine-tuning.

The resulting method, Layerwise Importance Sampled AdamW, or LISA, applies importance sampling across model layers and randomly freezes most middle layers during optimization. This changes which parts of the model are updated while keeping memory costs low. The approach makes the layer-level allocation of training updates the main mechanism for balancing adaptation and resource use.

Across the reported settings, LISA uses similar or less GPU memory than LoRA and can outperform both LoRA and full parameter training. The authors report MT-Bench improvements over LoRA of more than 10%–35%, with comparable or better results on MMLU, AGIEval, and WinoGrande. Results on LLaMA-2-70B also favor LISA over LoRA on MT-Bench, GSM8K, and PubMedQA, supporting its usefulness across the tested domains.
neurips-2024-lisa-layerwise-importance-s.tldr: LISA reduces fine-tuning memory by sampling layer updates and freezing most middle layers, with strong reported performance relative to LoRA.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning approximately optimal strategies in zero-sum games where players have incomplete information. Players learn from trajectories observed over repeated episodes. Existing procedures often use importance sampling across action sequences, which can produce high-variance estimates and make learning less stable.

The authors instead obtain observations through a fixed sampling policy while continuing to update the strategies being learned. Their algorithm applies Online Mirror Descent locally at each information set, a collection of game situations that a player cannot distinguish. Each local update uses its own decreasing learning rate and a regularized loss, allowing adaptation to occur separately across the game's decision points.

The analysis establishes a high-probability convergence rate proportional to the inverse square root of the episode count, up to logarithmic factors. Near-optimal dependence on game parameters requires the best theoretical choices of learning rates and sampling policies. To prove these results, the authors generalize mirror-descent stabilization to handle time-varying regularization with convex increments, connecting the local update design to its formal learning guarantees.
neurips-2024-local-and-adaptive-mirror-d.tldr: Local adaptive mirror descent with fixed-policy sampling provides high-probability convergence guarantees for learning strategies in imperfect-information games.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can struggle when a prompt assigns multiple attributes to multiple objects. Generating the requested objects is insufficient if their properties become mixed up. This paper investigates how the CLIP text encoder contributes to that attribute-binding problem, focusing on the representations passed from language processing to image generation.

The authors identify attribute bias in the text representation space and a contextual problem in padding embeddings that entangles different concepts. They introduce Magnet, a training-free method that uses positive and negative binding vectors to improve separation between the intended associations. A neighbor strategy further improves binding accuracy, making representation adjustment the central intervention.

Experiments show significant improvements in both synthesis quality and attribute-binding accuracy, with negligible additional computational cost. The authors also demonstrate generation of unconventional and unnatural concepts. These findings connect a practical image-generation improvement to specific properties of the text encoder: better separation of object-attribute associations in its representations helps the diffusion model follow more complex prompts.
neurips-2024-magnet-we-never-know-how-te.tldr: Magnet adjusts text representations without training to improve how diffusion models bind attributes to the intended objects.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy captures ensembles of macromolecules whose structures may vary. Some variation comes from a molecule adopting different conformations; other variation comes from the sample containing different protein complexes altogether. The paper addresses reconstruction when both forms of heterogeneity occur together, a setting that existing methods do not adequately model.

Hydra represents structures as arising from one of K neural fields and performs reconstruction from scratch. It must jointly infer the molecular structure, viewing pose, compositional class, and conformational state associated with the observations. A hybrid optimization strategy supports this combined inference, allowing the representation to account for both different molecular identities and structural variation within them.

The authors demonstrate Hydra on synthetic mixtures of proteins with substantial conformational variability and on an experimental cellular-lysate dataset containing different protein complexes. These demonstrations support a broader scope for heterogeneous reconstruction. The contribution is a more expressive way to model complex mixtures, extending reconstruction beyond variation within a single biomolecular complex to samples with multiple complexes.
neurips-2024-mixture-of-neural-fields-fo.tldr: Hydra uses a mixture of neural fields to reconstruct cryo-EM samples containing both different protein complexes and varying conformations.

paragraphs: Protein structure predictors such as AlphaFold2 depend on strong multiple sequence alignments, or MSAs, which organize related protein sequences together. This creates a challenge for proteins with few available homologous sequences. The paper addresses that bottleneck by generating additional sequence-alignment material to enrich what is already available.

MSA-Generator is a self-supervised protein language model trained on a sequence-to-sequence task using an automatically constructed dataset. It uses protein-specific attention mechanisms to draw on large protein databases and produce virtual MSAs. These generated alignments supplement existing ones, placing the contribution in the information supplied to structure predictors rather than in a replacement for those predictors.

Experiments on the CASP14 and CASP15 benchmarks report significant improvements in LDDT scores for both AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold. The gains are particularly notable for complex and challenging sequences. The findings support using a generative protein model to strengthen alignment inputs, with the practical benefit appearing in the accuracy of downstream structure prediction on the evaluated benchmarks.
neurips-2024-msa-generation-with-seqs2se.tldr: MSA-Generator creates virtual sequence alignments that improve reported AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold structure predictions.

paragraphs: Omnidirectional images capture a full 360-degree view, but their geometry differs from ordinary perspective images. Directly applying a perspective rasterizer to them can severely distort a Gaussian-splat reconstruction. ODGS introduces a rendering pipeline designed around this geometric difference while retaining the speed advantages of 3D Gaussian splatting.

For each Gaussian, the method constructs a plane tangent to the unit sphere and perpendicular to the viewing ray toward its center. A perspective rasterizer projects the Gaussian onto that local plane. The projected results are then transformed and combined into the omnidirectional image. This geometric interpretation exposes assumptions in the pipeline, which the authors examine through mathematical proofs.

The implementation parallelizes rasterization with CUDA and reports optimization and rendering speeds 100 times faster than NeRF-based methods. Across the evaluated datasets, ODGS delivers the best reconstruction and perceptual quality reported in the comparison. Experiments on roaming datasets also demonstrate recovery of fine details in large scenes, supporting the value of adapting the projection geometry specifically to omnidirectional input.
neurips-2024-odgs-3d-scene-reconstructio.tldr: ODGS adapts Gaussian rasterization to 360-degree geometry, delivering strong reconstruction quality and large reported speed gains over NeRF methods.

paragraphs: A single 3D detector trained across datasets must handle substantial differences between point clouds. Indoor and outdoor scenes can differ in scale and context, while datasets can use different object categories. The paper presents OneDet3D, which addresses these sources of interference within one framework using a single set of model parameters.

A routing mechanism guides domain-aware partitioning in scatter and context to reduce interference between data domains. Language-guided classification incorporates text to bring different datasets' label spaces into a common framework and mitigate category interference. A fully sparse architecture and an anchor-free detection head further accommodate point clouds whose scales differ substantially.

The experiments demonstrate broad detection capability across domains with one trained model, including diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. The authors describe coverage of almost all 3D detection tasks in their presented scope. The approach matters because it addresses several distinct obstacles to joint training together: differences in the input data, differences in category definitions, and differences in spatial scale.
neurips-2024-one-for-all-multi-domain-jo.tldr: OneDet3D combines domain-aware routing and language-guided classification to support indoor and outdoor 3D detection with one parameter set.

paragraphs: PANORAMIA measures privacy leakage through membership inference: attempting to distinguish examples that participated in a model's training from examples that did not. A common requirement for such measurement is access to non-training examples drawn from the same distribution. That requirement can make an audit dependent on data beyond the training records available to the auditor.

The framework uses generated data as its non-member examples. This removes the common dependency on a separate supply of in-distribution non-members. It requires access to a subset of the training data and leaves the model, training dataset, and training process unchanged. The audit therefore does not require retraining the model or altering how it was originally learned.

The authors evaluate PANORAMIA on image and tabular classification models as well as large-scale language models. The contribution is a change in the data requirements and procedure for measuring leakage across these model settings. Generated comparison examples make membership-based auditing possible under the stated access arrangement, while the access to some actual training examples remains part of that arrangement.
neurips-2024-panoramia-privacy-auditing-.tldr: PANORAMIA uses generated non-member examples to audit privacy leakage without retraining, requiring access to a subset of training data.

paragraphs: Appropriate responses to speech depend on more than the words spoken. Emotion, speaker characteristics, and background sounds can all contribute to what a dialogue system should understand. SD-Eval provides a benchmark for evaluating whether models use this additional information when understanding spoken dialogue and generating responses.

The benchmark combines material from eight public datasets and covers emotion, accent, age, and background sound. It contains 7,303 utterances totaling 8.76 hours. The authors implement three models and build a separate training collection using a similar process, containing 724,400 utterances and 1,052.72 hours. This supports evaluation of response generation under different information conditions.

Models conditioned on paralinguistic and environmental information outperform their counterparts on both objective and subjective measures. The evaluation also compares traditional text metrics, including BLEU and ROUGE, with human judgments and language-model-based metrics. The latter correlate more strongly with human evaluation in the experiments, suggesting that both the information given to a dialogue model and the way its responses are assessed matter.
neurips-2024-sd-eval-a-benchmark-dataset.tldr: SD-Eval tests spoken responses beyond word content and finds benefits from conditioning models on speaker and environmental information.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization objectives formed by subtracting one maximized function from another. These objectives can be both nonsmooth and nonconvex, making them difficult to optimize directly. The studied structure assumes that each maximized function is weakly convex and that the underlying functions are strongly concave in their respective maximization variables.

The authors introduce SMAG, a stochastic method based on approximate gradients of Moreau envelopes, which provide smoothed versions of the functions. Its central step estimates those gradients using only one stochastic gradient update of the primal and dual variables. This produces a single-loop algorithm for problem families that previously lacked one, including differences of weakly convex functions and weakly convex, strongly concave min-max problems.

The paper supplies a state-of-the-art non-asymptotic convergence rate, describing progress at finite computational budgets. Experiments on positive-unlabeled learning and partial ROC-area optimization with an adversarial fairness regularizer validate the method empirically. The contribution combines a simpler update structure with formal convergence analysis for the specified optimization assumptions.
neurips-2024-single-loop-stochastic-algo.tldr: SMAG provides a single-loop stochastic optimization method with convergence guarantees for structured differences of weakly convex functions.

paragraphs: Language models can generate false or biased content even after alignment. This paper proposes spectral editing of activations, or SEA, as an additional intervention applied while the model runs. It acts on internal representations, using demonstrations of desirable and undesirable behavior to determine how those representations should be adjusted.

SEA projects input representations into directions that maximize covariance with positive demonstrations while minimizing covariance with negative ones. Truthful and hallucinated outputs are examples of the two kinds of demonstrations. The authors also extend the method beyond linear editing through feature functions, broadening the transformations available for steering the model's internal activity.

Experiments cover truthfulness and bias benchmarks with six open-source language models spanning different sizes and families. The authors report superior effectiveness, generalization to similar tasks, and computational and data efficiency. They also find only a limited negative effect on other capabilities. The results support inference-time representation editing as a useful addition to existing alignment methods, while retaining the reported qualification that effects on other capabilities are limited rather than absent.
neurips-2024-spectral-editing-of-activat.tldr: SEA edits model activations at inference time using positive and negative demonstrations, improving reported truthfulness and bias outcomes.

paragraphs: UniAudio 1.5 explores whether a frozen language model can perform audio tasks through a few demonstrations. The central challenge is representation: audio is not naturally expressed in the textual vocabulary the model already understands. The paper addresses this with LLM-Codec, an audio codec designed to place audio into that existing vocabulary space.

LLM-Codec represents audio tokens using words or subwords from the language model's vocabulary while maintaining high reconstruction quality. The authors frame this representation as a new foreign language that the model can learn to use from examples in its context. Task adaptation therefore happens through demonstrations without updating the frozen language model's parameters.

Experiments examine speech emotion classification, audio classification, text-to-speech generation, speech enhancement, and other audio tasks. With only a few examples, the resulting system performs effectively in simple scenarios. This supports the proposed route to cross-modal in-context learning within that stated scope: the codec makes audio accessible to existing language-model capabilities, and examples specify the task to perform.
neurips-2024-uniaudio-1-5-large-language.tldr: UniAudio 1.5 encodes audio into a language model's vocabulary, enabling few-shot audio tasks with a frozen model in simple scenarios.

paragraphs: Vitron aims to bring visual understanding, generation, segmentation, and editing into one system for both images and videos. Its focus on pixel-level information addresses the difficulty of working precisely with visual regions rather than relying only on coarse descriptions of objects or whole scenes.

The architecture combines a language-model backbone with frontend encoders for images, videos, and regional visual inputs. Specialized visual models serve as backend components. To invoke those components precisely, Vitron communicates through both discrete textual instructions and continuous signal embeddings. This hybrid interface lets the language model pass information in two complementary forms when coordinating visual tasks.

Training includes pixel-level spatial and temporal vision-language alignment, alongside a cross-task module intended to strengthen fine-grained features shared across tasks. The authors demonstrate the system on twelve visual tasks and evaluate it across twenty-two datasets, covering its four main task groups. The contribution is a unified architecture and training approach for coordinating broad visual capabilities while retaining detailed regional information.
neurips-2024-vitron-a-unified-pixel-leve.tldr: Vitron combines a language model with visual encoders and specialist backends to support detailed image and video understanding and creation.

paragraphs: Vript expands video annotation from brief content descriptions to detailed, script-like accounts. Its dataset contains 12,000 high-resolution videos and captions for more than 420,000 clips, averaging about 145 words per clip. The annotations describe camera operations, including shot types and camera movements, as well as what appears in the scene.

Using this richer material, the authors explore three training paradigms for aligning more text with video. They produce Vriptor, a video-captioning model reported to rank highly among open-source models and perform comparably to GPT-4V. It can also generate dense, detailed captions for long videos end to end, extending the approach beyond isolated clip descriptions.

The paper additionally introduces Vript-Hard, with three tasks targeting demanding aspects of video understanding. Vript-HAL evaluates hallucinated actions and objects; Vript-RR combines reasoning and retrieval to resolve ambiguous long-video questions; and Vript-ERO evaluates temporal understanding of events in long videos. Together, the dataset, model, and benchmark address both richer video-language training and more demanding evaluation of the resulting capabilities.
neurips-2024-vript-a-video-is-worth-thou.tldr: Vript provides detailed video scripts, supports a strong captioning model, and introduces tests of hallucination, reasoning, and long-video temporal understanding.
